analogy.p: Imagine running downhill into a headwind that gets stronger the faster you run. At the start there is almost no wind against you, so you speed up quickly. As you speed up the wind pushes back harder, so you speed up more slowly. Eventually the push of the wind exactly matches the pull of the slope and you run at a steady speed, your terminal velocity. If someone opens a big umbrella, the wind pushes much harder, you slow down, and you settle at a lower steady speed. The analogy breaks down because the 'pull' down the slope is not constant for a runner as it is for gravity's pull on a skydiver, and real wind does not depend on your speed in the same way as fluid drag.
analogy.t: Running into a headwind that gets stronger

bullets: **Weight = mass x gravitational field strength (W = m g)**, with g = 9.8 N/kg near the Earth's surface; weight is measured in newtons (N).
The acceleration of free fall is **9.8 m/s2**, numerically equal to the gravitational field strength (9.8 N/kg).
A **free-falling** object has only its weight acting, so the resultant force is its weight and a = g.
Velocity increases by about 9.8 m/s every second of free fall (after 1 s: 9.8 m/s, after 2 s: 19.6 m/s).
Heavier and lighter objects fall at the same rate **if drag is negligible or absent**.
On the Moon g is smaller (about 1.6 N/kg), but the same idea applies: no atmosphere, no drag, no terminal velocity.
Link: Newton's second law, resultant force = mass x acceleration (F = m a), is used throughout this topic.
core.p: Near the Earth's surface an object falling freely, with no other forces acting on it, accelerates downwards at about **9.8 m/s2**. This is the same for all objects, whatever their mass, because a larger mass has a larger weight but also needs a larger force to accelerate it, so the two effects cancel (a = F / m = mg / m = g). In a vacuum a hammer and a feather really do fall together, as was shown on the Moon. In air, the difference in how objects fall is entirely caused by **air resistance**, not by gravity.

bullets: **Drag acts in the opposite direction to the motion**, so for a falling object it acts **upwards**.
Drag is a **resistive force** (resists motion) that transfers energy to the thermal energy stores of the object and the fluid.
Drag **increases with speed**: the faster the object moves, the greater the drag.
Drag depends on the **shape** (streamlined shapes have less drag) and on the **cross-sectional area** facing the fluid (larger area, more drag).
Drag also depends on the **fluid**: it is much greater in water or oil than in air, because there are many more particles in the way.
At the instant an object starts moving from rest, **drag is zero** (the speed is zero).
A **fluid** is a liquid or a gas, so the same ideas apply to a ball bearing falling in oil and a skydiver in air.
Link: drag, friction and upthrust are all contact forces; weight is a non-contact force.
core.h: Drag: the resistive force from a fluid
core.p: When an object moves through a **fluid** (a liquid or a gas such as air), the fluid exerts a force on it that acts **in the opposite direction to the motion**. This is called **drag** (air resistance when the fluid is air, and water resistance in water). It is a type of friction, and it is a **contact force** because it comes from collisions between the object and the particles of the fluid. Drag is the key force that stops a falling object accelerating for ever.

bullets: Slow object: fewer collisions with fluid particles each second and each collision is gentler, so drag is small.
Fast object: many more collisions every second, each with more momentum change, so drag is large.
For many everyday objects, drag increases roughly with the **square of the speed**, so doubling the speed gives about four times the drag (you do not need to calculate this at GCSE).
The force-speed graph for drag is a **curve that gets steeper**, while the weight is a **horizontal line**.
Where the curve crosses the weight line, **drag = weight**, which defines the terminal velocity.
Because the weight is constant and the drag changes, the resultant force changes as the object speeds up.
Use the phrase 'as the speed increases, the drag increases' in explanations rather than 'the air gets thicker'.
core.p: As an object falls it pushes aside the fluid particles in front of it. At a higher speed, **more particles are hit each second** and each is hit **harder**, so a larger force (in the opposite direction) is needed to push them aside and the drag force on the object is greater. This is why the drag grows quickly as the speed rises, and why there is always some speed at which the drag becomes large enough to equal the weight.

bullets: **Stage 1: just after jumping.** Speed is almost zero, so drag is almost zero. Resultant force = weight (downwards). Acceleration = g = 9.8 m/s2.

**Stage 2: speeding up.** As the speed increases, drag increases. Weight is still bigger than drag, so there is still a resultant force downwards, but it is **getting smaller**, so the acceleration is **decreasing** (speed still increasing).

**Stage 3: terminal velocity.** Drag has increased until **drag = weight**. The resultant force is **zero**, so acceleration is zero and the skydiver falls at a **constant velocity** (about 50 to 60 m/s if spread out, depending on body position).
**Stage 4: parachute opens.** The area increases greatly, so drag suddenly becomes **much bigger than weight**. The resultant force is **upwards**, so the skydiver **decelerates** (slows down).
**Stage 5: slowing down.** As the speed falls, the drag decreases, until **drag = weight** again at a much smaller **terminal velocity** (a few m/s).
**Stage 6: landing.** The skydiver falls at the new, smaller terminal velocity until reaching the ground, where the ground stops the motion.
Throughout, the **weight stays the same**; only the drag changes.
Note the skydiver is always still falling downwards after the parachute opens; slowing down does not mean going upwards.
core.h: The stages of a skydive, step by step
core.p: A skydiver's fall is the standard example, and examiners expect you to describe it **in stages, saying which force is bigger and what happens to the speed**. Weight is the same throughout (the mass does not change) and acts downwards. Drag acts upwards and changes. The motion follows from the resultant force: if the resultant force is downwards the skydiver speeds up, if it is zero the speed is constant, and if it is upwards the skydiver slows down.

bullets: At terminal velocity: **weight = drag** (balanced forces, resultant force = 0).
The object is still **moving downwards**; it falls at a constant speed in a straight line.
**Zero acceleration** does not mean zero velocity. Say 'no resultant force, so no acceleration'.

Terminal velocity is reached when the **speed is large enough for the drag to equal the weight**; a heavier object needs more drag so reaches a higher terminal velocity (if shape and area are unchanged).
Each shape and orientation has its own terminal velocity (e.g. a skydiver falling head-down compared with spread-eagled).
A falling object cannot exceed its terminal velocity in the same conditions, because drag would then exceed weight and slow it down.
Link: **Newton's first law**, balanced forces mean constant velocity; **Newton's second law**, F = m a.
core.h: Terminal velocity: definition and why the resultant force is zero
core.p: **Terminal velocity** is the **maximum constant velocity** that an object reaches when falling through a fluid, when the **drag (resistive force) is equal in size and opposite in direction to the weight**, so the **resultant force is zero**. Newton's first law then says the object continues at a constant velocity: it does not stop moving, it just stops accelerating. Newton's second law gives the same result: a = resultant force / mass = 0 / mass = 0.

bullets: Parachute open: **larger area, so larger drag at any given speed**.
Immediately after opening: **drag > weight**, resultant force **upwards**, so the diver slows down.
The deceleration is **greatest at the moment of opening** (the biggest resultant force) and decreases as drag falls.
Drag decreases as speed decreases, until **drag = weight**: resultant force zero, **constant lower velocity**.
The new terminal velocity is much smaller (a few m/s) than before opening (tens of m/s).
The weight of the skydiver does not change when the parachute opens.
Link: stopping distance and impact force: a lower speed on landing means less kinetic energy to dissipate, so a safer landing.
core.p: When the parachute opens, the **surface area** facing the air increases suddenly, so for the same speed the **drag increases a lot**. Drag is now bigger than weight, which gives an upwards resultant force, so the skydiver **decelerates**. As the speed falls the drag falls, until it is equal to the weight again, and a **new, lower terminal velocity** is reached. This lower speed is what makes it safe to land.

bullets: **Start of the fall:** the line is steepest, with a gradient of 9.8 m/s2 (acceleration = g); drag is zero.
**Curve getting shallower:** acceleration is decreasing because drag is increasing, so the resultant force is decreasing.
**Horizontal line:** gradient = 0, so acceleration = 0, **terminal velocity**; weight = drag.
**Sudden fall in the line when the parachute opens:** a negative gradient, so deceleration; drag > weight.
**Second horizontal section:** the new, lower terminal velocity; weight = drag again.
**Area under the graph** = distance fallen (count squares, Higher tier).
To find the acceleration at a point on a curved section, draw a **tangent** and find its gradient (Higher tier).
Say 'the velocity is still increasing but at a decreasing rate' for the curved part; do not say 'it is slowing down'.
core.p: On a **velocity-time graph** the **gradient is the acceleration** and the area under the line is the distance travelled. For a skydive the graph is a curve that starts steeply and then flattens out to a horizontal line, then drops and flattens at a lower value. You must link each part of the graph to the forces. A decreasing gradient means the acceleration is decreasing, which means the resultant force is decreasing, which means drag is increasing towards the weight.

bullets: **Weight (N) = mass (kg) x 9.8 N/kg.** An 80 kg skydiver has W = 80 x 9.8 = **784 N**.
**Resultant force = weight - drag** while speeding up (downwards positive); resultant = drag - weight after the parachute opens (upwards positive).
**Acceleration = resultant force / mass** (a = F / m), in m/s2.
Example: drag 240 N: resultant = 784 - 240 = 544 N downwards; a = 544 / 80 = **6.8 m/s2**.
At terminal velocity drag = 784 N for the same skydiver (resultant = 0).
Parachute opens, drag 3000 N: resultant = 3000 - 784 = 2216 N upwards; a = 2216 / 80 = **27.7 m/s2** upwards (a deceleration).
Always include units (N, m/s2) and a direction in the final statement if asked.
While the object is still **speeding up**, its acceleration is never more than g (it starts at g and falls); the deceleration after a parachute opens can be much larger than g.
core.h: Calculating resultant force and acceleration during the fall
core.p: You can use the stages to do numerical work. First find the weight with W = m g. Then take the drag value from the question. The **resultant force is the difference between weight and drag**, with the larger one deciding the direction. Finally, use **a = F / m** to find the acceleration. Take care with directions: take downwards as positive during the fall and say clearly which way the resultant acts.

bullets: **Larger weight (greater mass), same shape:** higher terminal velocity, because a bigger drag is needed to balance a bigger weight.
**Larger cross-sectional area:** more drag at each speed, so a **lower** terminal velocity.
**More streamlined shape** (head-down, pointed): less drag at each speed, so a **higher** terminal velocity.
**Denser fluid** (water or oil instead of air): more drag, so a much **lower** terminal velocity.
Spreading out arms and legs increases area; diving head-first reduces area.
A flat sheet of paper has a lower terminal velocity than the same sheet scrunched into a ball because of the larger area.
Stacking several coffee filters increases weight but the area stays similar, so the terminal velocity is higher.
Always link the answer to 'drag = weight' to get the full marks.
core.p: Terminal velocity is reached when drag equals weight, so anything that changes the weight or changes how much drag is produced at a given speed changes the terminal velocity. A **larger weight** needs a larger drag to balance it, which needs a higher speed. A **larger area or less streamlined shape** gives more drag at each speed, so the balance happens at a lower speed. This is why skydivers can change their fall speed by changing their body position.

bullets: **Ball bearing in oil:** large drag, so terminal velocity is reached after a short distance; the distance-time graph becomes a straight line.
**Raindrops:** reach terminal velocity, so they hit the ground at a safe speed rather than at the high speed a free fall from cloud height would give.
**Car at top speed:** the forward driving force is equal to the drag, so the resultant force is zero and the speed is constant.
**Cyclist:** at a constant speed on the flat, the driving force equals the resistive forces (air resistance plus friction).
**Feather and hammer on the Moon:** no atmosphere, no drag, no terminal velocity, both accelerate at the same rate.
**Bubbles rising** in liquids and **dust settling** also move at constant speed once drag (and upthrust) balance the weight.
**Parachute design:** a large area canopy produces high drag to give a low landing speed.
core.h: Other examples: liquids, rain, cars and cyclists
core.p: Terminal velocity applies to any object moving through a fluid with a driving force or weight, not just skydivers. A ball bearing dropped in a tall cylinder of oil or washing-up liquid reaches a constant speed quickly. Raindrops fall at a constant speed for most of their fall, which is why they do not hurt. A car or cyclist has a similar balance between the driving force and drag, which sets a top speed.

bullets: Gravitational potential energy lost = m g h (J) for a fall through height h.
Kinetic energy = 1/2 m v2 (J); at terminal velocity this does not change.
Work done against drag = drag force x distance (W = F s), which heats the air and the object.
This is a closed-system energy conservation idea: total energy is conserved, but not all of it ends up in the kinetic store.
Why parachutists land safely: the kinetic energy at the lower speed is far less than it would be at the first terminal velocity.
Higher tier: the energy dissipated is wasted energy, spread to the surroundings and not usefully stored.
core.p: When an object falls, its **gravitational potential energy store** decreases. Before terminal velocity, some of this energy transfers to the **kinetic energy store** (the object speeds up) and some is transferred to the **thermal energy store** of the surroundings by work done against drag. At terminal velocity the speed is constant, so the kinetic energy is constant, and **all of the energy lost from the gravitational store is transferred to the thermal energy stores** of the air and the object by the work done against drag.

bullets: **Independent variable:** e.g. the number of filter papers (mass) or the area of the parachute; **dependent variable:** the terminal velocity or the time to fall a set distance.
**Control variables:** drop height, shape, release method, the fluid, and the temperature of the oil.
Use a **video camera** and a ruler, or **light gates** and a data logger, to reduce reaction time error compared with a stopwatch.
Repeat several times and take a **mean** to reduce random error; ignore clear anomalies.
On a distance-time graph, a curve followed by a straight line shows acceleration then terminal velocity; the speed = the gradient of the straight section.
Mark the cylinder with equal spacing (for example every 10 cm) and time each interval; equal times for equal intervals show terminal velocity.
Safety: clear spills of oil, as they are slippery, and use a tray to catch the ball bearings.
Accuracy limits: parallax when reading marks, release technique, air currents.
core.p: Terminal velocity can be investigated with **coffee filter papers** dropped from a fixed height, or with a **ball bearing falling through a tall cylinder of oil or glycerine**. The idea is to measure distances and times and then plot a graph; once the line becomes straight on a distance-time graph the object is at terminal velocity and the gradient is the terminal velocity. The investigation tests your ability to name variables, reduce errors and decide on the measurement method.

bullets: **Resultant force > 0, downwards:** speeding up; graph curves upwards with a positive gradient; stage 1 and 2.
**Resultant force = 0:** constant velocity; horizontal line; terminal velocity.
**Resultant force upwards:** slowing down; negative gradient; parachute just opened.
**Newton's third law** pairs: the skydiver pushes the air down, the air pushes the skydiver up; these act on different objects and are not the 'balanced' weight and drag.
**Momentum:** a change in momentum equals the force x time; this applies to landing too.
**Stopping distance** and **braking** also use ideas about resistive forces and energy dissipation.
Higher tier: be ready to use areas and tangents on the graph with data, not just a sketch.
core.h: Links to other topics and exam-ready summary
core.p: Terminal velocity ties together almost the whole of the forces topic. It uses **weight**, **resultant forces**, **Newton's first and second laws**, **velocity-time graphs** and **energy stores**. In exam questions, the whole skill is to move between the story (what is the skydiver doing), the graph (what shape is it) and the forces (which is bigger). Practice linking the three in a table until it is automatic.

exam: **Command words:** 'describe' = give the stages and say what the speed does; 'explain' = give the forces and say which is bigger and why; 'calculate' = show W = m g and F = m a with units.
**1 mark:** a statement such as 'weight is equal to drag' or 'resultant force is zero' or 'the acceleration decreases'.
**2 marks:** one idea fully linked, e.g. 'drag increases as speed increases (1) until drag = weight, so the resultant force is zero (1)'.
**3 marks:** often a calculation: W = m g, resultant = W - drag, a = F / m, each with correct values and unit.
**4 marks:** describe a v-t graph with forces: acceleration, terminal velocity, parachute, new terminal velocity, mention gradient or forces for each part.

**6 marks (extended):** a chain of reasoning through at least four stages: initial acceleration g, drag increases, resultant decreases, terminal velocity, parachute opens, drag > weight, slows, lower terminal velocity. Use the words 'resultant force', 'drag', 'weight', 'terminal velocity'.
**Model phrases:** 'weight is constant', 'drag increases as speed increases', 'resultant force is zero', 'acceleration is zero so velocity is constant', 'larger surface area so greater drag'.
Draw arrows of the **correct relative lengths** in force diagrams: equal at terminal velocity, drag longer after the parachute opens.
Do not say 'gravity stops' or 'forces stop'; say 'the forces are balanced'.
On graph questions, quote the **gradient** for acceleration and say which part is terminal velocity (horizontal line).
For Higher tier tangent questions, draw a large triangle on the tangent and write down the values.
Check the final speed or acceleration is sensible: terminal velocities of tens of m/s for a skydiver, a few m/s with a parachute.

mistakes.r: There are still two forces, weight and drag, but they are equal and opposite so the resultant force is zero.
mistakes.w: At terminal velocity there are no forces acting.

mistakes.r: It keeps moving at a constant velocity; the acceleration is zero, not the velocity.
mistakes.w: At terminal velocity the object stops moving / the speed is zero.

mistakes.r: The weight stays the same all the way down; it is the drag that increases until it equals the weight.
mistakes.w: Gravity gets weaker or stops as the object falls.

mistakes.r: Without drag all objects accelerate at the same rate (g); in air the difference is due to drag, and the terminal velocity depends on weight and area.
mistakes.w: The heavier object falls faster because gravity is stronger on it.

mistakes.r: The skydiver is still moving downwards but slows down, because the resultant force (drag > weight) acts upwards.
mistakes.w: When the parachute opens the skydiver goes upwards.

mistakes.r: At terminal velocity drag is equal to weight (balanced forces).
mistakes.w: Drag is greater than weight at terminal velocity.

mistakes.r: The velocity is still increasing; the acceleration (gradient) is decreasing because drag is increasing.
mistakes.w: The skydiver slows down on the curved part of the graph because the line flattens.

mistakes.r: Drag increases because the speed increases, so more air particles are hit each second and harder.
mistakes.w: Air resistance increases because the air gets thicker lower down.

mistakes.r: The weight is unchanged; the parachute increases the area and so the drag.
mistakes.w: The parachute makes the weight smaller.

mistakes.r: Calculate the weight with W = m g (80 x 9.8 = 784 N) before comparing it with drag.
mistakes.w: Using mass instead of weight in force balances (e.g. 80 = drag).

summary: The specification asks you to explain that an object falling through a fluid (such as a skydiver in air) first accelerates because of the force of gravity, that its drag increases with speed until the resultant force is zero, and that it then falls at a constant terminal velocity. You must be able to draw and interpret velocity-time graphs for objects reaching terminal velocity, with the forces on the object at each stage. It matters because it pulls together weight, resistive forces, Newton's laws and graphs in one of the most commonly examined contexts.

terms.d: The constant velocity reached by an object falling through a fluid when the resistive force (drag) is equal to the weight, so the resultant force is zero.
The resistive force on an object moving through a fluid, acting in the opposite direction to the motion.
Drag when the fluid is air.
A liquid or a gas, whose particles can flow.
The force acting on an object due to gravity; weight = mass x gravitational field strength, in newtons.
The force per unit mass in a gravitational field, about 9.8 N/kg on the Earth surface.
Falling with only the force of gravity acting; acceleration is about 9.8 m/s2 near the Earth.
The single force that has the same effect as all of the forces acting on an object together.
The rate of change of velocity; a = change in velocity / time; also a = F / m.
A negative acceleration: a decrease in speed.
Forces that cancel each other out so the resultant force is zero.
Shaped so that the fluid flows smoothly past, giving a smaller drag.
The area of the object facing the direction of motion, which affects the drag.
A graph of velocity against time; the gradient is the acceleration and the area under it is the distance travelled.
A straight line that touches a curve at one point; its gradient gives the rate of change at that point.
Moving at the same speed in the same direction, which needs a zero resultant force.
An object at rest stays at rest and a moving object continues at a constant velocity unless acted on by a resultant force.
Acceleration is proportional to the resultant force and inversely proportional to the mass; F = m a.

worked.q: A skydiver of mass 80 kg is falling and, at one moment, the drag on her is 240 N. Gravitational field strength is 9.8 N/kg. Calculate her acceleration at this moment. [4 marks]
steps: Weight = m g = 80 x 9.8 = 784 N (1 mark).
Resultant force = weight - drag = 784 - 240 = 544 N downwards (1 mark).

worked.ans: (a) Resultant force 2216 N upwards; acceleration 27.7 m/s2 upwards (she slows down). (b) 784 N.
worked.q: The same skydiver opens her parachute and the drag becomes 3000 N. (a) Calculate the resultant force and her acceleration. (b) What is the drag when she falls at the new terminal velocity? [5 marks]
steps: Drag is greater, so resultant = 3000 - 784 = 2216 N upwards (1 mark).
a = 2216 / 80 = 27.7 m/s2 (1 mark), directed upwards so she decelerates (1 mark).
At the new terminal velocity the resultant force is zero, so drag = weight = 784 N (1 mark).

worked.ans: When she leaves the aircraft her speed is low so the drag is small and the resultant force (her weight) is large downwards, giving an initial acceleration of about 9.8 m/s2. As her speed increases the drag increases, so the resultant force and acceleration decrease, although the speed still increases. Eventually the drag equals her weight, the resultant force is zero and she falls at a constant terminal velocity. When the parachute opens the area is much larger so the drag is suddenly much greater than her weight; the resultant force acts upwards and she decelerates. As she slows, the drag decreases until it again equals her weight; the resultant force is zero again and she falls at a much lower constant terminal velocity until she lands.
worked.q: Explain the changes in the velocity of a skydiver from the moment she leaves the aircraft until she lands safely with the parachute open. [6 marks]
steps: Initially only weight acts, resultant force = weight, acceleration = g.
As speed increases, drag increases, resultant force decreases, acceleration decreases.
Parachute opens: area increases, drag > weight, decelerates.
Drag falls as speed falls until drag = weight again.
